item.title: The Bugs Were Our Own Linker Wraps: Making a PHP Timeout Actually Time Out
item.description: In the stack guard post the villain was a -Wl,--wrap linker flag that turned off PHP’s C-stack overflow guard. It wasn’t the only one. Until August, max_execution_time did nothing in ePHPm on Linux, for the same reason: we had wrapped the function that arms it to a no-op. A runaway script ran until the HTTP layer’s request timeout gave up on it and sent a 504, and the PHP thread kept burning CPU after that.

item.title: We Disabled PHP's Stack Guard Ourselves: Containing Segfaults in a Single-Process PHP Server
item.description:
php-fpm has a property nobody thinks about until they leave it: when a worker segfaults, you lose one request. The master forks a new child and life goes on. ePHPm runs every tenant’s PHP as threads inside one process. That’s where the memory and latency wins come from, and it also means one tenant’s segfault takes down every other tenant on the box.

This is the story of closing that gap, in four steps over about two weeks. The last step turned out to be a bug we’d put there ourselves. It’s also the payoff for the thread pool work in the previous post: everything below that actually shipped depends on ePHPm owning its own PHP threads.

item.title: PHP Signal Safety - The Init Ordering Bug Nobody Warns You About
item.description:
Last week I wrote about why ePHPm embeds PHP from Rust and promised the signal bug its own post. Here it is. It’s the kind of bug where the fix is about ten lines and the explanation is the whole post, because nothing in PHP’s embed documentation (there’s barely any) tells you that initializing PHP has process-wide side effects that assume PHP is the only thing in the process.
